rows.description: A toddler rubs eyes, tugs at ears or presses the face into a parent when sleepy, hungry or unwell. The cue is ambiguous, so a caregiver checks the whole picture, such as feeding time, fever or noise, rather than one sign.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A toddler sucks a thumb, twirls hair or strokes a blanket when tired or worried. These movements settle the nervous system and are a typical comfort; they usually fade with age and need no shaming.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A toddler climbs into a lap, cuddles or holds a hand to seek comfort and closeness. This is a core way of feeling safe; warm, responsive touch supports secure attachment, and a child who pulls away should be respected.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A toddler pushes, hits or grabs when frustrated, without the words to say no or mine. It signals anger or a strong wish, not cruelty; calm limits, naming the feeling and teaching gentle hands are the wise response.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Approaching and staying near a caregiver [Expressing]
rows.description: A toddler stays within sight of a parent, returns for reassurance and moves off to explore. Closeness shows attachment and safety seeking, and a child who wanders away without checking back deserves supervision.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A toddler turns away, hides or turns toward a parent when a new person approaches. It signals wariness rather than rudeness; adults who wait, keep a gentle distance and let the child approach help trust grow.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A toddler giggles at peekaboo, tickles or silly faces, and laughs more when a caregiver joins in. Early laughter signals delight and social bonding; it also can come from nervous surprise, so watching for cues of comfort is wise.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: joy, amusement, playfulness, anxiety

rows.subtype: Laughing at a fall or a shock [Mismatch]
rows.description: A toddler may laugh after a bump or a scare, while looking to a parent for a reaction. It can be relief, confusion or imitation, not callousness; a calm response shows the child whether the moment was safe.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: amusement, confusion, surprise, relief

rows.subtype: Bawling from distress or unmet need [Expressing]
rows.description: A toddler bawls loudly with hunger, pain, fatigue or fear; it is the strongest alarm signal available. A calm, quick, soothing response builds trust and teaches that distress can be relieved.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: fear, relief, tiredness, calm

rows.subtype: Crying as a signal of need [Expressing]
rows.description: A toddler cries from hunger, pain, tiredness, fear or frustration, and different cries may sound different. Crying is a communication of need, not manipulation; a warm, prompt response teaches trust.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: sadness, anger, fear, tiredness
